pages.x: By 500 the Western Roman Empire was gone. Vandals ruled North Africa from Carthage, Ostrogoths ruled Italy and Visigoths Spain. In Constantinople the emperors of the East still called their realm the Roman Empire, and in 527 a man came to the throne who meant to make it whole again: Justinian.

In 532 the chariot-racing fans of Constantinople rioted, burned much of the city, and crowned a new emperor. Justinian was ready to flee, but his wife, Theodora, a former actress, said, it is told, that royalty makes a fine burial shroud. He stayed, and his general Belisarius massacred thousands of rioters in the Hippodrome.

In 533 Belisarius sailed for Africa with about 15,000 men in 500 ships. He routed the Vandal king, Gelimer, at Ad Decimum, entered Carthage the next day, and in 534 Gelimer surrendered. Led in triumph through Constantinople, he kept repeating, it was said, the words of the Bible: "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity."

In 535 Belisarius took Sicily almost without a fight, then crossed to Italy, stormed Naples and entered Rome in December 536. The Goths besieged him there for a year, and failed. In 540 they offered to make him emperor of the West; he pretended to agree, Ravenna opened its gates, and the Gothic king was taken captive to Constantinople.

Just as a terrible plague began to sweep the empire in 541, the Goths chose a brilliant new king, Totila. He won back most of Italy, freeing slaves and winning over peasants to his side, and in 546 starved Rome into surrender. Belisarius came back with too few men, and was recalled again in 549.

At last Justinian gave a large, well-paid army to Narses, a eunuch of the palace in his seventies. In 552, at Taginae, his archers cut down the Gothic cavalry, and Totila was killed. The last Gothic king fell near Vesuvius that autumn, and in 554 Narses destroyed an army of Franks. Italy was Roman again.

In Ravenna, won back from the Goths, the church of San Vitale was finished in 547. Its glittering mosaics show Justinian and Theodora, with haloes, bringing gifts to the altar among their courtiers and guards: the most famous portraits of the age.

Twenty years of war, famine and plague had wrecked Italy, and Rome, taken and retaken again and again, was a shadow of itself. In 568, three years after Justinian's death, the Lombards invaded and took much of the peninsula for good.

Africa, Italy and a strip of southern Spain were Roman again, and the Mediterranean was almost a Roman lake once more. But the wars had cost too much, and the empire, worn down by plague, could not hold its gains: the Lombards soon took most of Italy, and the Arabs, later, Africa.
